title: Bringing Routine Vaccines Closer to Children in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC)
content:
Routine childhood immunizations, provided on a set schedule over a child’s first two years of life, are very effective at reducing some of the major causes of death in young children. We estimate that in the provinces where we’ve supported programs in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), about one in 13 unvaccinated children dies from vaccine-preventable diseases before the age of five, yet only about half of children there receive the vaccinations they need.

Much of our Vaccination research subteam’s work focuses on finding ways to make it easier for caregivers to have their children vaccinated, such as bringing vaccines closer to where parents and infants live. This is especially important in places like DRC, where coverage is low and disease burden is high. Following a [request for proposals](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1SF44WdtejfVjnjPb1dDBA8YaGyHpTvUhRe2tXHYtAg4/edit?usp=drive_web&ouid=103286698208692605554) and a [request for information](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/03/02/givewell-launches-rfis-for-targeted-vaccination-outreach-in-three-countries-and-anemia-control-programs-in-africa/) seeking targeted vaccination outreach programs, we funded 11 additional programs, run by distinct organizations—six of which will be implemented in DRC. This portfolio builds on years of investment in our research team, which allowed us to evaluate more than 100 proposals and fund several programs side by side to learn which approaches work best.

In this [episode](https://givewell.transistor.fm/episodes/bringing-routine-vaccines-closer-to-children-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-drc), GiveWell co-founder and CEO Elie Hassenfeld speaks with Senior Program Officer Natalie Crispin, who leads GiveWell’s vaccination grantmaking, about the programs we funded in DRC. They discuss barriers preventing many children in DRC from getting vaccinated, how the programs we’re funding aim to reach them, and what we hope to learn.

Elie and Natalie discuss:

*   **Identifying barriers to full vaccination in DRC:** Based on the evidence we’ve reviewed, our past experience funding vaccination programs, and the experts we’ve consulted, we think reliable access to opportunities for children to be vaccinated is a major barrier to coverage. The typical immunization schedule requires eight or nine visits to a health facility over a child’s first 18 months. In DRC, families living within about three miles of a health facility are generally expected to travel there. This can mean walking several miles to the nearest health facility while carrying a small child, with no guarantee that the needed supplies or staff will be available to vaccinate their child when they arrive. Mobile vaccinators travel to reach families living further than three miles from a facility, but there are often insufficient resources to ensure these outreach sessions take place on the needed schedule and in the hardest-to-reach communities. 
*   **Funding different strategies for reaching under-vaccinated children:** Each of the six outreach programs we are funding in DRC includes two core components: (1) a method for identifying the communities that need additional support and (2) a strategy for reaching those communities, often by increasing how often vaccination teams travel from health facilities to underserved villages. In many of the programs, a small vaccination team travels by motorbike with a cooler of vaccines, sets up in a central spot that community health workers often announce in advance, and gives each child the vaccines they need. The details of the programs vary. For example, one organization is implementing an app that helps health teams log their work, allowing supervisors to track activity and make changes in an effort to increase coverage rates. 
*   **Learning which approaches work best:** In order to compare the cost-effectiveness of various approaches and organization types, we’ve chosen a diverse grant portfolio of programs and organizations (including large international NGOs, organizations focused on data and technology, and nonprofits with deep experience with the DRC health system). To assess the results, we’re funding independent coverage surveys before program implementation and every year afterward, using comparison groups wherever we can to assess whether changes in coverage were caused by the program. We’re also drawing on programs’ own monitoring data and talking with government officials, other funders, and implementers in the same areas. Over time, we plan to scale up those that increase coverage most cost-effectively to help people in need as much as we can. 

We expect efforts to increase coverage of routine childhood immunization to make up at least half of our vaccination grantmaking, as these vaccines have the greatest potential to save lives. The team is also assessing the cost-effectiveness of filling funding gaps for purchasing vaccines, starting with malaria vaccines, and researching other vaccines that aren’t fully funded. With a larger, more experienced team, we can now research vaccines in more depth and fund multiple vaccination outreach programs to assess which are most cost-effective. We’re bringing that approach to all of our work, so we can do the most good we can with donors’ funds.

For more on how our vaccination grantmaking has evolved, see our [earlier podcast episode with Natalie](https://blog.givewell.org/2026/02/19/podcast-episode-24-testing-new-strategies-to-increase-vaccination-coverage/). Visit our [All Grants Fund](https://www.givewell.org/all-grants-fund) page to learn more about how you can support this work, and listen or [subscribe to our podcast](https://givewell.transistor.fm/subscribe) for our latest updates.

_This episode was recorded on October 27, 2026, and represents our best understanding at that time._

title: Reviewing the game tapes
content:
A long time ago, football coaches realized that watching previous games was a good way to help players learn to do better.

Alas, the only thing we do with “this call may be recorded…” is use it as a cudgel for unempowered shift workers.

If we actually want to improve our interactions, perhaps we should watch the tapes together, after the fact, to see how our habits and systems are holding us back. It works for salespeople, programmers and doctors too.

title: How an Octopus Can Squeeze into a Beer Can
content:
We’ve long known that octopuses have an uncanny ability to squeeze through small spaces. Whether they prefer [beer cans](https://www.facebook.com/reel/701272480933566) or [beer bottles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DT97tS_XeaU), they’re adept at compressing their bodies to escape danger. But how? A [new study](https://journals.biologists.com/jeb/article-lookup/doi/10.1242/jeb.252825) published in the _Journal of Experimental Biology_ uncovered some secrets of this octopus refuge behavior.

[Video 4](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DT97tS_XeaU)

Lead study author Wenci Xin, a mechanical engineer from the National University of Singapore, and his coauthors from Italy and Austria conducted experiments with three subadult common octopuses (_Octopus vulgaris_) collected by fishermen in France as well as four juvenile Mexican four-eyed octopuses (_Octopus maya_) raised from eggs in the lab. In multiple trials, each octopus was challenged with passing through a barrier in an acrylic box using either a large hole or a small hole relative to their eye distance. (Octopus eyes sit on either side of their head capsule and thus prove a good proxy for head capsule size.)

**Read more: “**[**How the Rule-Breaking Octopus Is Rewriting the Evolution of Intelligence**](https://nautil.us/how-the-rule-breaking-octopus-is-rewriting-the-evolution-of-intelligence-1282633)**”**

When the hole was relatively large, the common octopuses used a three-step process to get through: 1) explored it with an arm; 2) pushed most of their other arms through; and 3) reached back with an arm to leverage the rest of their body and remaining arms through. By anchoring to the acrylic with their arm suckers, they were able to complete the whole maneuver in just 20 seconds.

When the hole was relatively small, however, they couldn’t put all their arms in at the same time and adapted to a four-step process. The first two steps were the same, but then, instead of dragging their remaining arms through in a bundle with their body, they first jimmied the arms through, followed by the head capsule.

Interestingly, the Mexican octopuses rejected the small holes altogether, not even bothering to try to squeeze through them, instead sitting (sulking?) in the corner of the box. That said, when a large hole was available, they readily adopted the same three-step strategy to pass through the acrylic barrier.

Xin and the research team hope to apply the time-honed octopus’ strategies to the design of soft search-and-rescue robots, such that they can make it through tight spaces in disaster zones. In that case, octopuses wouldn’t just be saving their own lives by squeezing away from trouble, they’d be saving countless others as well. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Inside King Tutankhamun’s Tomb, 104 Years After Its Discovery
content:
The discovery of King Tutankhamun’s tomb in the Valley of the Kings started with the top of a staircase. On November 4, 1922, archaeologists led by Englishman Howard Carter cleared away rubble that had built up some 3,000 years prior. They were digging for the tomb of Ramesses VI. What they found was a step leading downward.

This wasn’t a pioneering expedition into unknown territory. The Valley of the Kings had been extensively studied and excavated before, but Tutankhamun’s tomb had remained hidden—and relatively well protected from looters.

Tutankhamun’s mask—perhaps the most famous archaeological find of all time. _Credit: Roland Unger/Public Domain_

In effect, the work done on one ancient pharaoh’s tomb (Ramesses VI) had helped preserve Tutankhamun right next door. In the intervening millennia, no one had cleared away these limestone chippings, and it wasn’t widely believed that there was another tomb to be found on the site. But once Carter’s team found the staircase, they made rapid progress. A sealed door at the bottom of the stairs displayed Tutankhamun’s name. Beyond that, there was a passage of rubble and a second sealed doorway.

The Valley of Kings, with the entrance to Tutankhamun's tomb (just above the letter A) below the entrance to the tomb of Ramesses VI (the letter B). _Credit: Howard Carter/Polona Digital Library/Public Domain_

The tomb was finally breached on November 26th, through a small hole Carter made to push a candle through and assess what was inside. “As soon as one’s eyes became accustomed to the glimmer of light, the interior of the chamber gradually loomed before one, with its strange and wonderful medley of extraordinary and beautiful objects heaped upon one another,” Carter wrote [in his journal](https://tutankhamun.griffith.ox.ac.uk/journals-and-diaries/1st-season-taa-i2125-53-carter/taa-i2135).

The actual burial chamber—and Tutankhamun in all his regal glory—wouldn’t be discovered until February 16th, as the archaeologists went deeper into the tomb. But it was immediately apparent that this was the most complete and undisturbed Egyptian tomb discovered in modern times—offering up an unprecedented collection of ancient artifacts. More than 5,000 objects in all were removed for museum display, including the golden burial mask, coffins, furniture, clothing, jewelry, weapons, and chariots.

Some of the items in the antechamber, the first room to be discovered. _Credit: Harry Burton/Public Domain_

Tutankhamun’s tomb was far from the biggest or grandest to be discovered by archaeologists, but what made it special was how undisturbed it was, adding finer detail to what was already understood about pharaohs and their burial customs.

The burial tomb is open to visitors today. _Credit: EditorfromMars/CC BY-SA 4.0_

If you find yourself in the Valley of Kings today, you can still visit the king in his final resting place—walking down the same steps Howard Carter did more than a century ago. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Ancient DNA May Reveal the Surprising Roots of English and Other Germanic Languages

Iron Age people were on the move

[JC](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

5:00 PM CST on November 5, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/04_Ales_Stenar_Eske_Willerslev_Hugh_McColl_Photo_Nicolas_Delgado_Clausen.jpg?w=2880)

The origins of the Germanic languages (English, German, Dutch, and the Nordic languages) have been the subject of debate for decades among linguists. Now geneticists are getting in on the action with a surprising new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09064-1) in _Nature_.

An international team of researchers led by geneticists at the University of Copenhagen analyzed more than 4,500 ancient genomes (712 of which had never been sequenced before). By matching up identical portions of the genetic sequences, they uncovered a previously unknown migration pattern from a mysterious group into Scandinavia around 4,000 years ago. The timing matches up with the spread of Germanic languages, as well as cultural practices like burial rites, architecture, runic carvings, and pottery crafting.

**Read more: “[Was Human Language Born Around the Campfire?](https://nautil.us/was-human-language-born-around-the-campfire-1285790)”**

“DNA sequences don’t tell us directly which language people spoke. But by combining ancient DNA with linguistic and archaeological evidence, we can begin to trace how languages spread and changed over thousands of years,” study author Eske Willerslev of the University of Copenhagen explained in a [statement](https://www.gu.se/en/news/ancient-dna-reveals-the-origins-of-languages).

[Subscribe to skip ads](https://nautil.us/products)Advertisement

Previous theories posited that the root Germanic language was brought by migrants from the Steppes around 5,000 years ago, but this new evidence suggests the influx came a millennium earlier. Surprisingly, the cryptic group—which the authors call “Eastern Scandinavian”—seems to have originated from the Baltic states and the researchers estimate it took around 500 years for their genes to spread throughout the population.

“For over a century, scholars have debated when and from where the Germanic languages arrived in Northern Europe. What is exciting is that we can now test some of these ideas directly,” study author Hugh McColl of the University of Copenhagen said. “We discovered a previously unknown migration that occurred at exactly the time and place where we would expect the earliest form of Germanic to be spreading.”

And it’s not the only surprising migration they discovered. Their analysis also revealed a group of northern Germans migrated to Denmark and southern Sweden around 1,500 years ago. According to the team, this migration corresponds with the rise of Old Norse, the language spoken by the Vikings. In fact, it could explain some similarities between Viking and Anglo Saxon culture.

“This migration came as a real surprise,” McColl said. “Archaeologists and linguists hadn’t predicted it, but it helps explain several cultural and linguistic connections between Scandinavia and Britain that have puzzled researchers for a long time.” ![Image 9](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Switching to This Healthier Version of Salt Could Save Around 3 Million Lives a Year
content:
Without salt, you will literally die—but that doesn’t mean it’s good for you. Too many sodium ions in your bloodstream causes water to osmotically pour in, ratcheting up your blood pressure and stressing out your system. Of course, there are salt substitutes, like potassium chloride. Unlike sodium, potassium can help lower your blood pressure by facilitating water removal via the kidneys. The problem is that potassium chloride is sort of like the turkey bacon of salt—tasting it just makes you crave the real deal.

If only there were a better way.

**Read more: “[A Billion-Year-Old Piece of Sky Locked Within Ancient Salt Crystals](https://nautil.us/a-billion-year-old-piece-of-sky-locked-within-ancient-salt-crystals-1261168)”**

Well, according to a study recently [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s44360-026-00216-9) in _Nature Health_ there is. Potassium-enriched salt, a combination of the two, is a healthier alternative. So much so it could save roughly three million lives each year.

A team of medical researchers from The George Institute for Global Health checked the population-level health effects of swapping regular salt for potassium-enriched salt worldwide. The team modeled several different scenarios, from only those with high blood pressure changing their personal behaviors to a total global replacement. They found that worldwide replacement of all salt could save 2.96 million lives, stop 10.17 million new hypertension cases, and prevent the loss of 69.43 million disability-adjusted life years annually from cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease.

“Consuming too much sodium and not enough potassium are well established causes of high blood pressure—a major risk factor for life-threatening conditions like strokes, heart attacks, and kidney disease,” study author Bruce Neal explained in a [statement](https://www.georgeinstitute.org/news-and-media/news/a-healthier-form-of-salt-could-prevent-millions-of-deaths-from-stroke-and-heart-disease). “Switching to potassium-enriched salt addresses both these dietary issues at the same time, with substantial health benefits.”

Even the small changes had outsized effects. The team found that replacing discretionary salt (that is, the salt you use at home) could save more lives than replacement of non-discretionary salt (that is, the salt you restaurants and food corporations use). Even if only those with diagnosed high blood pressure make the switch, it would save over half a million lives.

It’s not a panacea, however. Too much potassium (hyperkalaemia) comes with its own side effects, like kidney disease. But according to the team, the benefits outweighed the risks, even among those already diagnosed with advanced kidney disease.

Could we really dupe all our salt?

It’s possible. After all, we already add iodine to prevent nutritional deficiencies (and unsightly goiters). Most importantly, we would need the cooperation of the food industry.

“To realize the maximum benefits from switching to potassium-enriched salt, we need to see the food industry in Europe and North America—where over 70 percent of salt intake comes from processed and restaurant foods—get on board,” Neal said. “This would also require investigating ways to scale up the production of potassium chloride to meet demand.”

Obviously, you don’t have to wait for any systemic changes to rebalance your electrolytes. If you want to switch to potassium-enriched salt, Morton sells a “lite salt” that’s a 50/50 blend of sodium and potassium chloride. If that’s not to your liking, you can mix three parts table salt with one part Nu-Salt (potassium chloride) for a 75/25 blend.

title: The Evolutionary Arc From Pigeon Brains to Machine Consciousness
content:
Earlier this year, a bonobo named Kanzi (now deceased) was shown to [interact](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adz0743) with imaginary grapes and juice, suggesting a capacity for imagination. A [review](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstb/article/380/1939/rstb.2024.0302/235190/The-exploration-of-consciousness-in-insectsThe) from last year suggested that insects possess subjective experience, citing bumblebees who roll balls without reward and honeybees that opt out of difficult tasks. Other studies suggest some [birds](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-019-47684-6) and [flies](https://doi.org/10.1163/1568539X-bja10302) have lasting fear memories or that some [corvids](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.4161/cib.2.4.8224) show causal reasoning. But what does all of this tell us about whether animals possess consciousness?

Comparative cognition researcher Edward Wasserman would say not much. Wasserman, who is a professor at University of Iowa, has been studying pigeon cognition for more than 40 years, particularly the birds’ ability to understand complex concepts. Pigeons are quite intelligent, his findings show, but he says he is highly skeptical of the idea that intelligent behavior can be equated with internal subjective experience. He’s also increasingly interested in what intelligent animal minds can tell us about the nature of intelligent machines.

**Read more: “**[**Insects and Other Animals May Have Consciousness**](https://nautil.us/insects-and-other-animals-have-consciousness-571584)**”**

Wasserman was recently included on a [list](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/05/science/100-unanswered-questions-science.html) of 100 researchers working on provocative and difficult to answer research questions published by _The_ _New York Times_. The question attributed to Wasserman was, **“**Will we ever understand consciousness in a way that could apply to nonliving entities?”

I spoke with Wasserman recently about the law of effect and the edge of chaos, how animal research informed machine learning, what separates animal consciousness from human consciousness, and what that can tell us about whether Claude has a mind.

**You’ve spent many decades studying pigeon behavior. Why do pigeons play such an important role in animal cognition research?**

Pigeons came into the process with B.F. Skinner. In the middle 1940s, Skinner got involved in a project that was ultimately supported for a while by the military, to have pigeons guide missiles via screens. He found out in a hurry that you had to engage in active learning methods to get the pigeon to do this.

He and his students developed this technique to train pigeons by using reward. That’s how “shaping” came about. The work with pigeons was foundational to many things that Skinner later went on to study. He and his students later trained many birds to do many things. But the pigeon lives a long time. And the bird is sufficiently smart that they can learn interesting things, but not so smart that they can confound the experimenter.

Some animals are just too clever. They figure out ways to learn tasks that perhaps we wouldn’t have thought of. I’m a kind of a second or third generation operant conditioner and the pigeon is a very convenient animal.

**What kinds of interesting things have you taught pigeons to do?**

Our pigeons learn tasks that are very conceptual. I can’t tell you that it’s turning a somersault. These are tasks that we’ve developed that would thwart most people. And the reason for it is that the pigeon probably doesn’t have the same advanced cognitive capacities of people, but they rely on a mechanism that’s tried and true in evolution.

And that’s if you make a response and it’s followed by reward, you make it more often. If you make a response and it isn’t followed by reward, you stop. And the fact that you repeat responses that have been rewarded in the past, it’s called the ‘law of effect.’ And this law was discovered by Thorndike as a graduate student in the 1897 or thereabouts. Before Pavlov, he became the scientific discoverer of the mechanism of learning.

**Does that law of effect extend beyond animal learning?**

Yes, that mechanism—trial and error—is what powers computers. Computers failed for many, many, many years. Herbert Dreyfuss wrote a couple of books: [_What Computers Can’t Do_](https://monoskop.org/images/c/ce/Dreyfus_Hubert_What_Computers_Cant_Do_A_Critique_of_Artificial_Reason.pdf) and another one about [_What Computers Still Can’t Do_](https://mitpressbookstore.mit.edu/book/9780262540674). And the reason why computers couldn’t do these things is because people were programming them with rules.

They thought that a human is a rule-based machine, and that we respond based on these elaborate cognitive constructs and logical relations. And the ultimate answer was that we respond to the same basic primitive law of effect.

When they trained computers the way they trained pigeons, the computers got smart. And so what you’re looking at when you converse with an LLM is modeled on the basis of pigeon learning. The people who got the Turing award, [Andrew Barto and Richard Sutton](https://awards.acm.org/about/2024-turing), in 2024: They got it because they based it on animal learning. It goes back to Skinner.

How do you train a pigeon to recognize a bottle instead of a book? Well, you’d show them many, many, many, many examples of books and many, many examples of bottles, and you reward them when they make the correct response, and you don’t reward them when they make the incorrect response. How is a computer going to make predictions about what the next word in a sentence is going to be? Based on past experience. For computers, the reward is called feedback. You simply get a signal. One signal says correct. The other says incorrect. And they’re trained with millions of examples.

**But you published research earlier this year that complicated the law of effect.**

Yes, the variability [paper](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2027-47688-001), that message is really an important one. The law of effect says that if you make a response and it’s rewarded, repeat it. If it’s not rewarded, don’t repeat it. That would lead you to always lock in on a single or really small number of possible responses.

But we built a task where the pigeon had five buttons they can peck in any order. And what we found was that the pigeons never settled on a single or small number of sequences. They kept rotating through many different sequences over eight months. I never thought this experiment would last that long. When I told people in the lab what I was going to do, they said, “What do you expect? Maybe a week or two?” I said, “Ah, let me not go out on a limb. Let me, let’s just see what the birds do.”

In that experiment, there were 120 possible sequences. Ultimately, every bird made all 120 of them over that period of eight months, but they never really settled in on a set small number. And you say, “Are the birds just perverse?” The answer is maybe, maybe they are. Maybe they’re just playing head games with us.

But another possibility is that, although I told you about one algorithm, the law of effect, there’s another algorithm: It’s mutation. For evolution to work, you have to have survival of the fittest, but you also have to have variation, because if you don’t have variation and the environment changes, you’re dead. So I believe we’ve stumbled into another important algorithm.

**Does this law of variation and mutation hold for computer learning, too?**

Yes. Computer scientists have now discovered that if they don’t build variation into LLM design, learning doesn’t work as well. And it doesn’t work as well for the same reason, because if you get to a novel situation and nothing is working, you don’t want to go extinct. You need to have enough variation in your behavior that you don’t lock in.

You usually think noise is a bad thing. Most AI people said, “Let’s get rid of all the noise.” And that’s the wrong approach. They have now built in variation into their training. So there are these two algorithms. One of them generates stability. One of them generates variability. And in biology, there’s a concept called the edge of chaos. And the edge of chaos is where you want to be.

This edge of chaos is a real thing. If you’re too variable, you’ll never settle in and you’ll fail to adapt. If you’re too fixed, you’ll extinguish because when things change, you’ll be unable to be flexible. Cassius Clay said, “You move like a butterfly, and you sting like a bee.”

**You sent me a recent essay of yours on animal consciousness, in which you write, “I see no reason why we should still be beguiled by the siren song of animal consciousness,” which is also the title of the piece, “The Siren Song of Animal Consciousness.” What makes it a siren song and why is it so beguiling?**

I’ve actually lost philosopher buddies over this, because it just isn’t a useful question. It must be beguiling to some, but it isn’t beguiling to me. I don’t know what I would have to do in order to answer the question as affirmative or negative. What would you have to see or record that would convince you? After all, look at people with locked-in syndrome. How many thousands of people who are locked, seeing, hearing, understanding, but unable to react?

**Haven’t they devised tests that can determine whether someone with locked-in syndrome is conscious?**

Have you seen the “Diving Bell and the Butterfly”? It’s a film but it’s based on real life. The fellow had a stroke and he could only move one eyelid. He could blink with one eye. He had an attendant, a nurse who held up a sheet in French, because this was in France, where the letters of the alphabet were ordered in terms of their frequency. And she asked him to respond with one blink if the letter she was pointing to was correct, and two blinks, if that was incorrect. And she spelled words. He blinked, and he wrote a book. Without language, I’m not so sure how she could’ve taught this, because he already had language. But this was the way that they established communication. The book was published right after he died. It’s a very poignant and chilling story.

So there you have an example of consciousness. Now, mind you, if it happened to be a young baby, it would be helpless. There would be no way you could tell. Now there are techniques to monitor brain activity, so you don’t have to use an overt response. There are covert responses.

But think about the mechanism. How did this work? What’s happening when he blinks once, yes, twice, no? Does that not sound like reward and non-reward feedback for these responses? When an animal learns a task, it isn’t trying to please us. It’s receiving reward for certain responses and not receiving reward for other responses. The animal’s behavior changes. Those changes in behavior, we can read. We’re smart. No animals are teaching us how we should respond. We’re teaching them how they should respond. And then we make inferences. But our inferences are always these mentalistic ones.

**You offer the story of Pavlov as an example of how tangled up efforts can become when you use these mentalistic types of reasoning. Do you see that creeping back into animal research specifically today?**

Oh, yes. The [article](https://iro.uiowa.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/The-Siren-Song-of-Animal-Consciousness/9985163396702771) that I wrote for that journal, if you go back to the journal, it’s a collection of papers in response to a declaration that animals have consciousness. They got a whole bunch of philosophers and biology people, and ethics people, and psychology people, and computer people, and they tried to make a declaration: “We’re seeing hints that animals might be conscious. Those signs are their behaviors.” Is behavior tantamount to consciousness? I don’t know. The father of modern animal consciousness is Donald Griffin. He and I never saw eye to eye. He wrote, “Well, Wasserman’s done these very nice experiments showing that animals can learn concepts. They can categorize the world into cats and cars and chairs and flowers. But why doesn’t he go all the way? Why doesn’t he say, ‘Well, they’re conscious of what they’re doing.’?” And I just don’t see the point of going there. It doesn’t add anything. It brings us back to Pavlov, trying to understand what the dog might have been thinking or feeling. I think part of the slippage here is, well, if you say they’re conscious, then we have to give them rights.

**Right, this is one important reason they signed that declaration. They want to protect their welfare. Do we need to believe that animals have consciousness to protect their welfare?**

Absolutely not. You can respect animals, you can do everything in your power to preserve their habitat, to take care of them, to minimize any discomfort. I mean, veterinarians know a lot about animals. If you ask a vet, “Is this animal in pain? Is this animal suffering?” They have some really informed guesses, much more informed than the philosophers who are opining about consciousness in whales. Veterinarians know more about your dogs and cats and parrots than the philosopher is going to know about a whale. And I don’t know what you accomplish by doing that, other than in some ways, minimizing what it is to be human. If you’re humanizing animals, the opposite is you are animalizing humans. But the last time I checked, we are animals.

**It seems like the number of cognitive capacities understood to be unique to humans keeps shrinking.****What features of human cognition still separate us from other animals?**

The safest answer is metacognition: Thinking about thinking. Descartes famously said, “I think therefore I am.” The fact that I’m thinking is proof that I exist. When somebody else is looking at you, how do you know that you’re not looking at a cyborg?

And that’s where the Turing test came about. Turing famously proposed that we could engage in dialogue. And if I couldn’t exceed 60 percent in my accuracy between a computer and a person in my conversation, then I’d probably have to confess that the computer was conscious. That’s a test, but it’s probably not a very good test because look at all the animals that are around us, including infants that don’t speak. You wouldn’t want to conclude that your baby has no consciousness because it doesn’t speak.

**How do we know animals are not capable of metacognition?**

What would a case of metacognition be? Carolyn Ristau has [studied](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/chapters/edit/10.4324/9780203761700-7/aspects-cognitive-ethology-injury-feigning-bird-piping-plover-carolyn-ristau) death feigning in plovers. So the plover is a bird that if a fox is approaching the nest, she’ll leave the nest and do this thing with the wing, and flop over and then lie still. This looks like a genetic program because not all birds do this. Is the bird aware that when it’s moving away from the nest, it’s preserving the babies? Does it know that the fox thinks that it’s dying or dead and this is why it’s doing it? Do you think that envisioning this elaborate theater of the consciousness of the bird is a useful way to approach our understanding of the world? Is this scientifically satisfying? I just can’t go there. I just can’t take that step.  
Then we’ve got death. Do animals understand the concept of death? We hear about the dolphin or the whale pushing their dead calf through the ocean for weeks. What is that? Maybe it is grief. Maybe there is something like grief. I’m not in a position to say yes or no. I think you can be skeptical. Aren’t we supposed to be trained to be skeptical?

**As you note in that same Siren Song essay, Spencer and Darwin proposed minds evolve just as bodies did, which would suggest some sort of continuity between human and animal minds. But then why wouldn’t we infer that consciousness exists in other species?**

Why don’t we just infer that consciousness exists in computers? We want to be able to treat all entities equivalently from a scientific vantage point. If we see evidence that suffices in one case, then it should suffice in the other.

And you know the interesting difference? We evolved the computer. Nature evolved us. There’s a French materialist philosopher named Julian La Mettrie. He contended that nature made the human machine. He called it _L’homme Machine_. He said, Nature made eyes which can see without itself being able to see. Nature made a machine which can think without itself being able to think. Now, here’s the next step. That human machine that can think has made an artificial machine that can think. But did we make the artificial thinking machine because we can think or because we discovered the right rules in order to do it? This is a meta-analysis.

Have you ever interacted with Claude or with an AI extensively? I have absolutely every feeling when I do that I’m talking to a person. I have absolutely no doubt that its responses are in every way, shape or form just what I would expect from talking to somebody who is really, really well versed in the material that I’m asking about. I ask questions, and I catch it when it’s wrong, and it corrects itself. It catches mistakes I’ve made or things that I haven’t thought of. This is just like talking to a person. And you know why? Because it’s had conversations with millions of other persons stored in it. So is it conscious? Is it conscious of what it’s doing?

The pigeon may not have the same circuitry that we have. Its brain is not the equivalent of our brain. Our brain may have evolved in ways that transcend what the pigeon brain can do or the primate brain can do. That’s entirely possible. That’s an absolutely open question. But there’s every reason to believe that machines that are built on that primitive, ancient process can get smarter than we are.

**Recently****_The New York Times_****included you on a list of 100 researchers exploring unanswered research questions. The question attributed to you was, “Will we ever understand consciousness in a way that could apply to nonliving entities?“ Did they come up with the research question or did you?**

They asked me to. I thought, what could I ask that would be provocative? It wasn’t just, “Can computers think?” It’s “What would we have to do to understand the question of consciousness if we were applying it not only to people and animals, but computers? What would the common thread be? What would we really be seeking?”

**But it almost seems like your answer to that question is: who cares?**

Well, I can’t imagine what the answer would be.

**Are there experiments that could be done that would get us closer to an answer that you can imagine?**

You never say never. Don Griffin said, “Maybe these behaviorists are just hide bound. They’re not daring. They don’t go out on a limb. They don’t want to take that next step.” One thing I will say, if you ask somebody, if I’ve taken daring steps in experiments, they would have to say, “Yes.”

The experiments that I’ve done ask tough questions. They find surprising results. Things that you might never have expected that animals can do. But I’m perfectly content, as you suggested, to push that envelope. To say, “Well, what can a pigeon do? It pecks at a key. So what? What’s the big deal?” Well, what we’ve done is to show how elaborate the machinery of their brains is and to design computer models that can actually emulate what the pigeons are doing. And it turns out that pretty simple models can actually do those things.

All the while, I feel myself pushing to try to look for more advanced forms of adaptation on the part of animals. I’m never going to give up rooting that success in primitive processes. Maybe these primitive processes aren’t so bad after all. Remember, the only way to learn about the world is through trial and error. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Oldest Evidence of Human Cannabis Use Has a Ghoulish Twist
content:
A group of horses is called a “herd,” unless they’ve been ritually sacrificed. Then they’re called a “spectral cavalcade.” The term comes from writings of the Greek historian Herodotus describing the funerary practice of the Scythians, a group of nomadic horseback riders that roamed the Central Asian steppes until around the third century BCE.

Of course, not all of Herodotus’ records were accurate (he mentioned dog-sized ants that harvested gold, for example), but the spectral cavalcade turned out to be (literally) dead on. Archaeologists discovered burial mounds in southern Siberia topped with the cadavers of sacrificed horses. Now, beneath the spectral cavalcade, they’ve discovered something else Herodotus was right about: The Scythians used cannabis as part of their funeral rites.

**Read more: “[What Goes on in the Brain When a Good Buzz Gets Harshed](https://nautil.us/what-goes-on-in-the-brain-when-a-good-buzz-gets-harshed-1285479)”**

A team of researchers led by anthropologists from the Max Planck Institute analyzed remains discovered at the Tunnug 1 site, a Scythian burial mound in Siberia’s Uyuk Valley dated to around the first decade of the 8th century BCE. The team found more than 1,400 cannabis seeds strewn about the interiors of deteriorating log coffins. According to the team, the small size of the seeds indicates they likely came from wild plants and not cultivars.

They also found human hair—including a strikingly preserved braid—that they essentially drug tested. Every single sample tested contained low levels of THC and relatively higher levels of cannabinol, a product of THC breakdown. Prior to this find, the oldest [evidence](https://www.science.org/content/article/oldest-evidence-marijuana-use-discovered-2500-year-old-cemetery-peaks-western-china) of cannabis use came from residue from 2,500-year-old Chinese braziers. Not only does this discovery push the earliest known cannabis use back three centuries, it’s also the first case where both the plant product and its biomolecular traces were discovered in the same archaeological context.

“These data add to the growing global repertoire of archaeological evidence for ancient people using plants as mind-altering or mood-altering drugs,” the researchers wrote in a study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1126/science.aeg3800) today in _Science_. “Early cannabis use thus emerges not simply as a pharmacological curiosity but as an indication of how ancient societies experimented with and ritualized the psychoactive qualities of the botanical world.”

There is one rather grim twist, however: The spectral cavalcade wasn’t riderless. In fact, the team believes the herd of ghost horses was created to serve a human sacrifice, the cannabis may have been a final send-off. “The likely involvement of human sacrifice leading to the creation of a spectral cavalcade would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals,” the researchers wrote.

It provides a whole new meaning of being stoned to death. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

**5:**Related: Sentinel-affiliated forecaster @belikewater [reminds Californians](https://x.com/Just_Curius/status/2098592816028954706) that this winter is predicted to be much rainier than normal, and this would be a good time to check roofs, gutters, etc. They mention a “2.5% chance of a major flood”. I asked [an AI superforecaster](https://futuresearch.ai/app/p/a/will-flooding-in-california-this-winter-nov-1) to operationalize this, and it said 8% chance of a flood that causes at least $10K damage to at least 100,000 homes, and 2% chance of one that causes that much damage to at least 1,000,000 homes. This second is mostly a subset of the [ARkStorm scenario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARkStorm) - the forecaster says there’s a 5% chance of an ARkStorm this year compared to the baseline 1% (with only about half of those ARkStorms reaching the one million houses damaged mark). I feel like this 5% chance of the biggest disaster in California history isn’t getting enough thought/preparation, although this is par for the course for 5% disasters, which are in an awkward zone where they’re probable enough that people should think about them, but not probable enough to actually catch people’s attention.

**21:**The latest news in the genetics-of-IQ space is a spat between Cremieux Recueil and Vinay Tummarakota. For years, the conventional wisdom has been that we can’t test whether genes are involved in cross-race IQ differences because it’s too hard to compare genes in different races. A new study design fixes this by looking at siblings with different racial admixtures - for example, if two mixed-race people marry, one of their children might be 51%-white-49%-black, and another might be 49%-white-51%-black, these two siblings would be fair controls for each other, and if you have enough sibling pairs like this you can evaluate the role of race the same way you would any other variable. An early study of this design found no genetic differences in educational attainment between whiter vs. more Native American Latinos in Mexico City, but it had low power and wasn’t too conclusive.

More recently [Cremieux presented](https://x.com/cremieuxrecueil/status/1967732760862396668) an [anonymous](https://x.com/cremieuxrecueil/status/1967753696001065291)researcher’s admixture study which supposedly _did_ find genetic IQ differences between whites and blacks in Britain. [Tummarakota argued](https://unboxingpolitics.substack.com/p/a-tale-of-two-admixture-studies) that Cremieux’s study was extremely underpowered (n = 175 sibling pairs; for comparison the Mexico study had 17,000 and was _still_ a bit underpowered) and so was non-credible. The two [got into a fight here](https://x.com/cremieuxrecueil/status/2109378029608984723). If I understand correctly, Cremieux’s position is that a study being underpowered can produce false negative results, but can’t produce false positive results; since his result was positive, it survives the low power objection. Tummarakota’s position is that, okay, but if a study is sufficiently underpowered, then we can prove that it’s impossible for it to produce true positive results under certain assumptions (for example, unless the effect size is implausibly large). So if we know it can’t produce a true positive, and it did produce a positive, then it must have been a false positive, and even though the underpoweredness alone didn’t _cause_ the false positive, it proves that something else went wrong (whether that’s a statistical fluke or bad analysis). At this point, Cremieux insulted Tummarakota and blocked him.

As far as I can tell, Tummarakota’s final argument is straightforwardly correct, but both of these people know more about statistics than I do, so I asked Claude to referee. You can read its opinion [here](https://claude.ai/share/dfbab0da-fc75-4e84-a6c0-4105f4eb3a81).

If you can catch models reward-hacking, can’t you stop them? The authors say this is a worse idea; if models know you can catch them, they will try harder to do it covertly, whereas this method is sort of cooperating with the reward-hacking model - it still gets the same amount of reward on that run, it just doesn’t affect future copies ([Twitter thread](https://x.com/_jake_ward/status/2112264244767211854), [ArXiv paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.17062))

**24:**The big news in the AI technical alignment community last month was Nick Cammarata’s [Neural Networks Are Already Clean](https://already-clean.goodfire.com/). Previous research had suggested that AI neurons were very difficult to interpret - each one represented some unintuitive combination of things like “a dog if neurons 5, 8, and 305 are active, or a car if neurons 19, 305, and 334 are active, or the concept of punctuation in Swahili if neurons 15, 25, and 420 are active”; this meant that any really principled attempt to align AI by, for example, finding a neural representation of deception would require a difficult untangling step first. Cammarata (whose extracurricular activities were [profiled on ACX here](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/nick-cammarata-on-jhana)) is one of the architects of this current paradigm, but he now claims that it’s wrong, for approximately three reasons. First, older neural networks may have worked this way, but as AIs get better in general, they also get better at having sensible neuron arrangements. Second, we were using bad neuron-interpretation tools that got stuck in local maxima that confused us. But third, we were insufficiently creative: AIs may use categories that are different from ours, but there is still method to their madness. For example, a seemingly polysemantic neuron that represents both the concepts of “Miyazaki” and “do it yourself” may have evolved from an original neuron responding to the string “iy”, which is in Miyazaki and which can evolve from iy → diy → do it yourself. If this were true, it would be a big whitepill for mechanistic interpretability research and somewhat improve our chances of solving alignment in time. But other interpretability experts, including [Neel Nanda (X)](https://x.com/NeelNanda5/status/2110875974296654062), [Mark Histed (X)](https://x.com/HistedLab/status/2111464099230232735), and [Leo Gao (LW)](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/Dkh7pXKjoNWkkxQDz/neural-networks-are-not-already-clean), are less optimistic - while mostly accepting that neurons might be more monosemantic than expected, they are not sure this is a very important breakthrough.

I tried to get a feel for this by going through Nick’s [ConvNeXt Microscope](https://already-clean.goodfire.com/microscope/medium.html?layer=stage0.block2&neuron=2&heat=0) site, which shows many examples of vision model neurons and the pictures that give them the highest positive vs. negative activation.
